title: Factorizations and minimality of the Calkin Algebra norm for \(C(K)\)-spaces
author: Antonio Acuaviva
abstract: For a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space \(K\), we prove that the essential norm on the Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K))/\mathscr{K}(C_0(K))\) is a minimal algebra norm. The proof relies on establishing a quantitative factorization for the identity operator on \(c_0\) through non-compact operators \(T: C_0(K) \to X\), where \(X\) is any Banach space that does not contain a copy of \(\ell_1\) or whose dual unit ball is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact. It follows that, for every ordinal \(\alpha\), the algebras \(\mathscr{B}(C[0,\alpha]))\) and \(\mathscr{B}(C[0,\alpha]))/\mathscr{K}(C[0,\alpha]))\) have an unique algebra norm.

1.

Introduction and Main Results

−
1.1.

Algebra norms, minimality and maximality of norms.

−

By an algebra norm on a (real or complex) algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) we mean a vector norm on \(\mathcal{A}\) which is submultiplicative. We say that an algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) admits an unique norm if any two algebra norms on \(\mathcal{A}\) are equivalent. We also have the weaker notion of admitting a unique complete norm, which simply says that any two complete algebra norms on \(\mathcal{A}\) are equivalent.

Central to uniqueness-of-norm problems are the notions of minimality and maximality of a norm. An algebra norm \( orm{\cdot}\) on \(\mathcal{A}\) is minimal (respectively, maximal) if for any other algebra norm \(\vertiii{\cdot}\) on \(\mathcal{A}\), there exists a constant \(c > 0\) such that \(c orm{\cdot} \leq \vertiii{\cdot}\) (respectively, there exists \(C > 0\) such that \(\vertiii{\cdot} \leq C orm{\cdot}\)). Observe that, if an algebra norm is both minimal and maximal, then it is the unique norm for the algebra \(\mathcal{A}\). Similarly, if a complete norm is either minimal or maximal, then the open mapping theorem gives that it is the unique complete norm.

Therefore, uniqueness-of-norm problems can be reframed as problems about the minimality and maximality of norms. These two problems are, in general, quite different. We shall focus on these problems for the Banach algebra \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) of bounded operators on a Banach space \(X\), as well as its quotients. We start by examining the problem of minimality of the norm.

Among the first results in this direction is a celebrated theorem of Eidelheit which states that, for any Banach space \(X\), the operator norm on the algebra \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) is minimal (and therefore it is the unique complete norm). A natural next step is to ask whether similar phenomena occur for quotients of \(\mathscr{B}(X)\), most notably the Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(X)/\mathscr{K}(X)\), where \(\mathscr{K}(X)\) denotes the ideal of compact operators. In this direction, Meyer showed minimality of the essential norm for \(X = c_0\) and \(X = \ell_p\), \(1 \leq p < \infty\). In his PhD dissertation, Ware undertook a systematic study of the uniqueness-of-norm problem for Calkin algebras, significantly extending Meyer's work. He proved the minimality of the essential norm for a large class of Banach spaces \(X\), including finite direct sums of \(c_0\) and \(\ell_p\) spaces, the infinite sums \(\left( igoplus_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \ell_p^n ight)_{c_0}\) and \(\left( igoplus_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \ell_p^n ight)_{\ell_q}\), Tsirelson's space \(T\) and its dual \(T^*\), and the James spaces \(J_p\) for \(1 < p < \infty\) . More recently, Johnson and Phillips have shown the minimality of the essential norm in the Calkin algebra for \(X = L_p\), \(1 < p < \infty\), while Laustsen and Arnott have shown minimality whenever \(X = C_0(K_\mathcal{A})\), where \(K_{\mathcal{A}}\) is a Mrówka space. For a broader and more in-depth perspective on this problem, we refer the reader to the recent paper by Arnott and Laustsen . For a more detailed discussion specifically in the context of Calkin algebras, we recommend the PhD thesis of Ware and the survey article by Skillicorn .

Our main result for the minimality problem is summarised in the following theorem.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and consider the Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K))/\mathscr{K}(C_0(K))\). Then the essential norm \( orm{\cdot}_e\) is minimal. In particular, the Calkin algebra admits a unique complete algebra norm.

The proof of the previous result is based on a bounding technique inspired by the Eidelheit-Yood method, as elegantly presented in Ware's thesis , together with a result about uniform factorizations of the identity on \(c_0\), Theorem 1.6, which we present later and believe may be of independent interest.

We now turn to the question of the maximality of norms. To highlight the contrast with the minimality problem, observe that while Eidelheit proved that the operator norm is minimal in \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) for any Banach space \(X\), an example of Read gives a Banach space such that the operator norm on \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) is not maximal (equivalently, there are spaces \(X\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) admits a discontinuous algebra homomorphism into a Banach algebra).

Observe that the maximality of the norm passes down to quotient spaces, while minimality does not. This is because the maximality of the norm is equivalent to proving that every homomorphism from the algebra into a Banach algebra is continuous. This characterisation explains why, when proving the maximality of the norm on a Calkin algebra, one usually focuses on proving the same question for the algebra of operators \(\mathscr{B}(X)\). This gives rise to the following natural question.

Is there a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space \(K\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) admits a discontinuous homomorphism into a Banach algebra?

Under the continuum hypothesis (CH), our previous question admits a positive answer if one drops the scattered condition, see , however, the space discussed there is far from being scattered. In upcoming work, we have managed to construct a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space \(K\) such that, under (CH), \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) admits a discontinuous homomorphism into a Banach algebra . The question remains open if the assumption on (CH) is dropped.

When dealing with this automatic continuity question for operator algebras \(\mathscr{B}(X)\), a famous theorem of B. E. Johnson shows that it is enough for the space \(X\) to be isomorphic to its square \(X \oplus X\) (or, more generally, to admit a continuous bisection of the identity). Nevertheless, this criterion alone proves insufficient for numerous spaces, even within the realm of continuous functions on scattered compact Hausdorff spaces. As an illustration, Semadeni showed that \(C([0, \omega_1])\) fails to be isomorphic to its square, where \(\omega_1\) represents the first uncountable ordinal. Even more, Loy and Willis went on to prove that this space cannot admit a continuous bisection of the identity, thus rendering Johnson's result inapplicable.

That being said, Ogden has proved that every homomorphism from \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \omega_\eta]))\), where \(\omega_\eta\) is the first ordinal of cardinality \(\aleph_\eta\) for an ordinal \(\eta\), to a Banach algebra is continuous. We provide a brief account of how Ogden's result extends to all ordinals \(\alpha\), yielding the following.

Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal. Then any homomorphism from \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \alpha]))\) into a Banach algebra is continuous.

The previous theorem, coupled with Theorem 1.1 and Eidelheit's theorem, gives a solution to the uniqueness of norm problem for the algebra of operators and the Calkin algebra on ordinal spaces.

Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal. Then the algebra of operators \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \alpha]))\) and the Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \alpha]))/\mathscr{K}(C([0, \alpha]))\) admit an unique algebra norm.

Lastly, we turn our attention to another property of interest in the study of algebra norms, namely Bonsall's minimality property, see . The formal definition is as follows, an algebra norm \( orm{\cdot}\) on an algebra \(\mathcal{A}\) has Bonsall's minimality property if \( orm{\cdot} = \vertiii{\cdot}\) whenever \(\vertiii{\cdot}\) is any other algebra norm on \(\mathcal{A}\) satisfying \(\vertiii{\cdot} \leq orm{\cdot}\). We obtain the following.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and consider the Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K))/\mathscr{K}(C_0(K))\). Then the dual essential norm \(T \mapsto orm{T^*}_e\) has Bonsall's minimality property.

1.2.

Quantitative factorizations of the identity.

−

Factorizations of idempotent operators play a prominent role in the study of the algebra \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) of bounded operators on a Banach space \(X\). For instance, such factorizations are central to the classification of the closed ideals of \(\mathscr{B}(X)\), and they also feature prominently in the study of the uniqueness of algebra norms. In our case, we will establish the following quantitative result.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and let \(X\) be a Banach space that does not contain a copy of \(\ell^1\) or for which the unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact. Then for any non-compact operator \(T: C_0(K) o X\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exist operators \(U \in \mathscr{B}(X, c_0)\) and \(V \in \mathscr{B}(c_0, C_0(K))\) such that

\[UTV = I_{c_0} \hspace{5pt} ext{ and } \hspace{5pt} orm{U} orm{V} < rac{2}{ orm{T}_e} + \varepsilon.\]

We also provide a further improvement of the previous theorem, namely, we show how the upper bound on the norms of the operators \(U\) and \(V\) is intimately related to the essential norm of the adjoint operator of \(T\), obtaining a characterisation of this norm.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and let \(X\) be a Banach space that does not contain a copy of \(\ell^1\) or for which the unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact. Then for any non-compact operator \(T: C_0(K) o X\)

\[ orm{T^*}_e = \sup \{ orm{U}^{-1} orm{V}^{-1}: UTV = I_{c_0} \}.\]

Theorem 1.6 could also be derived from Theorem 1.7 together with a duality result due to S. Axler, N. Jewell, and A. Shields . Although their result is stated only for the case where the domain and codomain coincide, a careful reading of the proof shows that it suffices for the dual of the domain to have the \(\lambda\)-metric approximation property for their argument to go through.

If \(K\) has an accumulation point, i.e. if \(C_0(K) ot = c_0(\Gamma)\), the constant \(2\) is sharp in Theorem 1.6, since in this case there exists an operator \(T \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) such that \( orm{T}_e = 2\) while \( orm{T^*}_e = 1\). Clearly, if \(C_0(K) = c_0(\Gamma)\) we have \( orm{T}_e = orm{T^*}_e\).

While our motivation regarding this factorization stems from the aforementioned paper of Arnott and Laustsen , the origin of the ideas predates significantly in time. The starting point is the following classical theorem of Pełczyński. Observe that when \(K\) is scattered, compactness and weak compactness coincide.

(Pełczyński )

Let \(K\) be a locally compact Hausdorff space and \(X\) be a Banach space. Then an operator \(T: C_0(K) o X\) is non-weakly compact if and only if \(T\) fixes a copy of \(c_0\).

We include a brief proof, based on the presentation in , as the reader may observe that the arguments in our proof of Theorem 1.6 constitute quantitative refinements of those presented therein.

ProofFold proof

Let \(T: C(K) o X\) be non-weakly compact. By Gantmacher's theorem, \(T^*: X^* o C(K)^*\), where \(C(K)^* = \mathcal{M}(K)\) is the space of all finite regular Borel measures on \(K\), is also non-weakly compact; that is, the bounded set \(T^*(B_{X^*}) \subseteq \mathcal{M}(K)\) is non-relatively weakly compact. By Grothendieck's classical characterisation of non-weak compactness in these spaces , there exist \(\delta > 0\), a disjoint sequence of open sets \((U_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) in \(K\), and a sequence \((x^*_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq B_{X^*}\) such that if \( u_n = T^*x^*_n\) then \( u_n(U_n) > \delta\) for all \(n \in \mathbb{N}\).

For each \(n\) we can find a compact set \(F_n \subseteq U_n\) such that \( u_n(U_n ackslash F_n) < \delta/2\). By Urysohn's lemma, there exists \(f_n \in C(K)\), \(0 \leq f_n \leq 1\) such that \(f_n = 0\) in \(K ackslash U_n\) and \(f_n = 1\) in \(F_n\). The map \(S: c_0 o C(K)\) defined by \(Se_n = f_n\) is an isometric embedding of \(c_0\) into \(C(K)\), where \((e_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is the canonical basis of \(c_0\).

Note that the operator \(TS: c_0 o X\) satisfies

\[\inf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} orm{TSe_n} \geq \inf_{n \in \mathbb{N}}|x^*_n(TSe_n)| = \inf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} |T^*x^*_n(f_n)| \geq \delta/2.\]

It follows from a result of Rosenthal (see , Remark 1 after Theorem 3.4), that \(TS\) is an isomorphism on a copy of \(c_0\), and thus the same holds for \(T\).

□

One can see from the proof that the value

\[\varepsilon(T) = \sup \left\{ \inf_n \left\| (T^* x_n^*)|_{U_n} ight\| : (U_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq K, (x_n^*)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq B_{X^*} ight\},\]

where the supremum is taken over all sequences of disjoint open sets \((U_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq K\) and all sequences \((x_n^*)_{n=1}^\infty \subseteq B_{X^*}\), quantifies how well \(T\) preserves a copy of \(c_0\). For the factorization, observe that the stability conditions on the codomain, i.e. that \(X\) contains no copy of \(\ell_1\) or that the unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact, are there to guarantee that for any copy of \(c_0\) we can pass down to a sub-copy that is complemented with good constants.

The essence of the proof of Theorem 1.6 lies in finding a lower bound for \(\varepsilon(T)\) in terms of the essential norm \( orm{T}_e\). Therefore, Theorem 1.6 can be interpreted as a quantitative version of Theorem 1.10. Since the groundwork for deriving the quantitative factorization from this was already explored and developed by Arnott and Laustsen , we focus on showing an equivalent condition, in the form of Theorem 3.3 (see Section 3).

In light of Pełczyński's theorem, one might hope that the assumption that \(K\) is scattered in Theorem 1.6 could be removed by replacing non-compactness with non-weak compactness. However, this is not possible, as \(\varepsilon( \cdot )\) is not comparable in general with the weak essential norm \( orm{\cdot}_w\). Details of this will appear elsewhere.

2.

Organization

−

We now outline the structure of the paper. Sections 3 to 7 present the proofs concerning the quantitative factorization of the identity on \(c_0\), while Sections 8 and 9 address the minimality and maximality of algebra norms.

In Section 3 we introduce some background material and terminology. Following the work of Arnott and Laustsen, we provide a reformulation of Theorem 1.6 in the form of Theorem 3.3, which we will use as our starting point for the proof. We provide a proof of Theorem 1.6 subject to the verification of Theorem 3.3.

Sections 4 to 6 work through the proof of Theorem 3.3. In section 4 we present some topological results, which allow us to introduce a particular class of projection operators. In the last part of this section, we will recall some properties of \(C_0(K)^*\), which will be needed moving forward.

Section 5 establishes the two main ingredients for the proof. First, in Proposition 5.2 we prove that we can find a sequence of functionals \((x^*_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset B_{X^*}\) which witness the action of \(T\) and that are almost orthonormal, in the sense that their weight is supported in a family of points \((F_j)_{j=1}^\infty\) which are disjoint.

The other ingredient deals with the accumulation of weight of an infinite collection of functionals. In particular, we establish that this weight cannot significantly accumulate on too many families of disjoint points. All of this is made precise in Lemma 5.4. Technical considerations make us restate this result in the form of Corollary 5.5.

Section 6 contains the proof of Theorem 3.3. The key step is an application of Corollary 5.5 and a diagonal argument to the family of functionals and points given by Proposition 5.2, which gives us a refinement of the functionals and points, with the added benefit that we can now separate the points via disjoint neighbourhoods. This is achieved in Lemma 6.1. The proof of the theorem then follows naturally.

Section 7 deals with the relation between the factorizations of the identity on \(c_0\) and the essential norm of the adjoint operator. This section contains the proof of Theorem 1.7.

Lastly, Section 8 focuses on the question of the minimality of the Calkin algebra norm, including a proof of Theorem 1.1, which is achieved via a simultaneous factorization of operators in the form of Lemma 8.2. This section also includes a proof of Theorem 1.5. In Section 9, we explain how to go from Ogden's result to Theorem 1.3.

3.

Preliminaries and proof of Theorem 1.6

−

All normed spaces and algebras are over the scalar field \(\mathbb{K}\), either the real or complex numbers, and we adhere to standard notational conventions. For a locally compact Hausdorff space \(K\), \(C_0(K)\) denotes the Banach space of continuous functions \(f: K o \mathbb{K}\) which vanish at infinity, in the sense that \(\{k \in K: |f(k)| \geq \varepsilon \}\) is compact for all \(\varepsilon > 0\), and equip it with the supremum norm.

We write \(B_X\) for the closed unit ball of a normed space \(X\) and denote by \(I_X\) (or \(I\) when \(X\) is clear from the context) the identity operator on \(X\).

The term “operator" will refer to a bounded linear map between normed spaces. As usual, given two normed spaces \(X\) and \(Y\), we denote by \(\mathscr{B}(X,Y)\) the collection of all operators from \(X\) to \(Y\); if \(X = Y\), we simply denote it by \(\mathscr{B}(X)\). Similarly, we denote by \(\mathscr{K}(X, Y)\) the ideal of compact operators, and for brevity we write \( orm{T}_e\) for the essential norm of an operator \(T \in \mathscr{B}(X,Y)\), namely

\[ orm{T}_e = orm{T + \mathscr{K}(X,Y)} = \inf \{ orm{T - S }: S \in \mathscr{K}(X,Y)\}.\]

More specialized notation will be introduced as and when needed.

In their work, Arnott and Laustsen established the following quantitative factorization result for the identity on \(c_0\) , which we restate below with notation adapted to our context.

(Arnott and Laustsen)

Let \(T \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K), X)\) where \(K\) is a locally compact Hausdorff space and \(X\) is a Banach space for which the unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact, and let \(\delta > 0\).

Then \(C_0(K)\) contains a sequence \((\eta_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\) such that

\[\sup_{k \in K} \sum_{n=1}^\infty |\eta_n(k)| \leq 1 \hspace{5pt} ext{ and } \hspace{5pt} \inf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} orm{T\eta_n} > \delta\]

if and only if there are operators \(U \in \mathscr{B}(X, c_0)\) and \(V \in \mathscr{B}(c_0, C_0(K))\) such that

\[UTV = I_{c_0} \hspace{5pt} ext{ and } \hspace{5pt} orm{U} orm{V} < 1/\delta.\]

In the previous theorem, we emphasise that \(\delta\) serves as the inverse of an upper bound for \( orm{U} orm{V}\). Consequently, an upper bound on \(\delta\) provides control over how small the upper bound for \( orm{U} orm{V}\) can be.

In their proof, Arnott and Laustsen note that the hypotheses can be relaxed to also include the case where \(X\) does not contain a copy of \(\ell^1\), provided that a result of Galego and Plichko can also be applied in the case of complex scalars. The only obstruction in the proof of Galego and Plichko is the verification of the following result of Hagler and Johnson in the case of complex scalars.

(Hagler and Johnson)

Let \(X\) be a Banach space. If \(X^*\) contains a closed subspace in which no normalized sequence converges weak\(^*\) to zero, then \(\ell^1\) is isomorphic to a subspace of \(X\).

We thank Professor W. B. Johnson for kindly explaining how the complex case follows from the real version of the theorem, and for permitting us to include his argument here.

ProofFold proof

Let \(X_\mathbb{R}\) be \(X\) when considered as a real Banach space. It is elementary that a sequence is weakly convergent (respectively, weakly Cauchy) in \(X\) if and only if it is weakly convergent (respectively, weakly Cauchy) in \(X_\mathbb{R}\). Therefore, by the complex version of Rosenthal's \(\ell_1\) theorem (due to Dor), it is enough to show that \(X_\mathbb{R}\) contains a copy of (real) \(\ell_1\). The map \(x^* \mapsto eal x^*\) is a real-linear, isometric, weak\(^*\)-to-weak\(^*\) homeomorphism of \(X^*\) onto \((X_\mathbb{R})^*\). Consequently, if the complex space \(X\) satisfies the hypothesis of Theorem 3.2, then so does the real space \(X_\mathbb{R}\). The real version of the theorem then gives that \(X_\mathbb{R}\) contains a copy of (real) \(\ell_1\) and thus, as previously explained, \(X\) contains a copy of (complex) \(\ell_1\).

□

Taking all of this into account, Theorem 1.6 will follow from the next theorem, whose proof we shall present in Sections 4 to 6.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space, \(X\) be a Banach space, \(T: C_0(K) o X\) be an operator with \( orm{T}_e = 1\) and \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\). Then there exists a sequence of disjoint functions \((\eta_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset B_{C_0(K)}\) such that \( orm{T\eta_j} > \delta\) for all \(j \in \mathbb{N}\).

4.

Topological preliminaries and \(C_0(K)\)

−

In this section, and throughout the rest of the paper, \(K\) will denote a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space. We observe that \(K\) is zero-dimensional, that is, there exists a base of clopen sets. To see this, note that \(K\) is scattered, hence totally disconnected, while from general topology we have that a locally compact Hausdorff space is zero-dimensional if and only if it is totally disconnected , thus our space \(K\) is zero-dimensional. Furthermore, since \(K\) is also locally compact, for every \(k \in K\), we can find a local base formed by clopen compact sets.

From now on, whenever we refer to a neighbourhood, we will always do so with the implicit understanding that it is clopen and compact. We denote by \(\mathcal{T}\) the collection of all compact and clopen subsets of \(K\), which is a base for the topology of \(K\).

Now we move to the idea of separating a finite family of points by a family of disjoint neighbourhoods. We make this precise in the next definitions.

A family of sets \(\mathcal{A}\) is called pairwise disjoint if \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) for any distinct \(A, B \in \mathcal{A}\).

Given a subset \(F \subset K\), we say that \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{T}\) is a neighbourhood collection around \(F\) if there exists a bijection \(U: F o \mathcal{U}\) such that \(k \in U(k)\) for each \(k \in F\).

Combining the previous definitions, we will say that \(\mathcal{U}\) is a pairwise disjoint neighbourhood collection around \(F\) if \(\mathcal{U}\) is a neighbourhood collection around \(F\) and it is pairwise disjoint.

We define the support of \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{T}\) as

\[S(\mathcal{U}) = igcup_{U \in \mathcal{U}} U,\]

in other words, the set of those points \(k \in K\) which belong to some member of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Since we shall mostly work with finite or countable collections of points and neighbourhoods, the following notation will be useful.

Let \(A\) be any set, we denote \( inset{A} = \{B \subset A: |B| < \omega\}\) and \(\inset{A} = \{B \subset A: |B| \leq \omega \}\), in other words, the collections of finite and countable subsets of \(A\), respectively.

Our next result is automatic given that the space \(K\) is Hausdorff.

Let \(F \in inset{K}\), then there exists a pairwise disjoint neighbourhood collection around \(F\).

Having introduced the necessary topological notions, we are ready to discuss an important class of operators on \(C_0(K)\).

Let \(F \in inset{K}\) and let \(\mathcal{U} \in inset{\mathcal{T}}\) be a pairwise disjoint neighbourhood collection around \(F\). We define

\[\proj(\mathcal{U}, F) = \sum_{k \in F} \delta_{k} \otimes \id{U(k)},\]

where \(\delta_k: C_0(K) o \mathbb{K}\) is the evaluation functional at \(k\), \(\id{U}\) denotes the indicator function of \(U\) and \(\delta_{k} \otimes \id{U(k)}\) denotes the rank-one operator defined via \(f \mapsto f(k)\id{U(k)}\).

Note that \(\id{U} \in C_0(K)\) because it vanishes at infinity since \(U\) is compact and it is continuous since \(U\) is clopen. Hence \(\proj(\mathcal{U}, F)\) defines an operator \(C_0(K) o C_0(K)\) with the following properties, whose verification is straightforward.

  1. \(\proj(\mathcal{U}, F)\) is a finite-rank projection.

  2. \( orm{\proj(\mathcal{U}, F)} = 1\), except in the trivial case where \(F = \emptyset\). Hence \( orm{I - \proj(\mathcal{U}, F)} \leq 2\).

  3. For any \(k \in F\), the adjoint projection satisfies \(\proj(\mathcal{U}, F)^* \delta_{k} = \delta_{k}\).

Finally, we shall need some properties of \(C_0(K)^*\). We start by recalling a well-known variant of Rudin's famous theorem . For completeness, we include a brief proof.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space. Then \(C_0(K)^* \cong \ell^1(K)\).

ProofFold proof

Let \(\alpha K\) be the one-point compactification of \(K\), adding the point at \(\infty\). Since \(\alpha K\) is also scattered, Rudin's theorem implies that \(C(\alpha K)^* \cong \ell^1(\alpha K)\).

Let \(\iota: C_0(K) o C(\alpha K)\) be the natural inclusion, so that \(\iota^*: C(\alpha K)^* o C_0(K)^*\) is an exact quotient map, meaning that it maps the closed unit ball onto the closed unit ball. Note that \(\ker{\iota^*} = \spn \delta_\infty\), where \(\delta_\infty\) is the evaluation functional at the point \(\infty\). Thus, the First Isomorphism Theorem gives

\[C_0(K)^* \cong C(\alpha K)^* / \ker{\iota^*} \cong \ell^1(\alpha K)/\spn {\delta_\infty} \cong \ell^1(K).\]
□

Let \(\mu \in C_0(K)^*\), we call the subset

\[\supp({\mu}) = \{k \in K: \mu(\{k\}) ot = 0\}\]

the support of \(\mu\).

Observe that given \(\mu \in C_0(K)^*\), we have \(\supp({\mu}) \in \inset{K}\) and

\[\mu = \sum_{k \in \supp{(\mu)}} \mu(\{k\}) \delta_k.\]

For \(C \subset K\), we define the restriction operator \(R_C: C_0(K)^* o C_0(K)^*\), acting on \(\mu \in C_0(K)^*\) by

\[R_C \mu = \sum_{k \in C} \mu(\{ k \})\delta_k.\]

It is easy to check that \(R_C\) is a projection operator with \( orm{R_C} = 1\) (except in the trivial case \(C = \emptyset\)). If one thinks of the space \(C_0(K)^* \cong \ell^1(K)\) as spanned by the transfinite Schauder basis \((\delta_k)_{k \in K}\), then the restriction operator \(R_C\) is the standard basis projection. Therefore, we have the following properties.

Let \(\{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_N\}\) be pairwise disjoint subsets of \(K\) and set \(C = igsqcup_{n=1}^N C_n\). Then:

  1. \(R_{C} = \sum_{n=1}^N R_{C_n}\), in particular, \( orm{\sum_{n=1}^N R_{C_n}} = orm{R_C} = 1\).

  2. For any \(\mu \in C_0(K)^*\), we have \( orm{\sum_{n=1}^N R_{C_n} \mu} = \sum_{n=1}^N orm{R_{C_n} \mu}\).

5.

Preliminary results

−

In this section, we introduce two ingredients that are key in the proof of Theorem 3.3. From now on, \(X\) will always denote a Banach space and \(T: C_0(K) o X\) an operator with \( orm{T}_e = 1\). Furthermore, for the rest of this section, we fix an arbitrary \(\delta \in (0, 1/2)\) and \( heta > 0\) small enough so that it satisfies \(2(\delta + 2 heta) < 1\).

if \(I_Y\) factors through \(T\) and \( u_Y{(T)} = 0\) otherwise. Further, let \(\mathcal{J}_Y = \{T \in \mathscr{B}(X): u_Y(T) = 0\}\), in other words, the set of operators that do not factor \(I_Y\). Observe that the set \(\mathcal{J}_Y\) is always closed.

Suppose that \(\mathcal{J}_Y\) is closed under addition (and thus, a closed ideal of \(\mathscr{B}(X)\)) and that \(Y\) admits a Schauder decomposition \((Y_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) with \(\sup \{d_{BM}(Y_n, Y) : n \geq 1\} < \infty\), where \(d_{BM}\) denotes the Banach-Mazur distance. Then \( u_Y\) minorizes any algebra norm on \(\mathscr{B}(X)/\mathcal{J}_Y\). In particular, if \( u_Y\) defines an algebra norm, it is minimal.

Further, note that the conditions on \(Y\) are satisfied, for example, by the classical sequence spaces \(\ell^p\), \(1 \leq p \leq \infty\).

These factorisation-type norms arise naturally in algebras of the form \(\mathscr{B}(X)/\mathscr{I}\) for some ideal \(\mathscr{I}\) and play a central role in the study of their norm properties. For example, in a forthcoming paper, Johnson and Phillips introduce the notion of uniform incompressibility (see also for a definition), and employ factorization-type norms to show this property holds in multiple Banach algebra of the form \(\mathscr{B}(X)/\mathscr{I}\). Our results show that the essential norm is uniformly incompressible for the Calkin algebra of \(C_0(K)\) spaces, \(K\) a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space.

Lastly, we provide a proof for Theorem 1.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.5Fold proof

Let \(\vertiii{\cdot}\) be any norm on \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K)) / \mathscr{K}(C_0(K))\) satisfying \(\vertiii{S} \leq orm{S^*}_e\) for all \(S \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\), we will show that then \(\vertiii{S} = orm{S^*}_e\) for all \(S \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\). For this, it is enough to show that \(\vertiii{S} \geq orm{S^*}_e\) for all \(S \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\).

So fix any non-compact operator \(T \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) and assume without loss of generality that \( orm{T^*}_e = 1\), we need to show that \(\vertiii{T} \geq 1\).

Choose \(A \in \mathscr{B}(c_0, C_0(K))\) and \(B \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K), c_0)\) according to Lemma 8.1 and fix any \(\varepsilon > 0\). By Theorem 1.7 we can find \(V \in \mathscr{B}(c_0, C_0(K))\) and \(U \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K), c_0)\) such that \( orm{U} orm{V} < 1 + \varepsilon\) and \(UTV = I_{c_0}\), which gives

\[AUTVB = AB.\]

Note that since \(I_{c_0} = BA\) then \((AB)^2 = AB ot = 0\), and thus

\[1 \leq \vertiii{AB} = \vertiii{AUTVB} \leq \vertiii{AU}\vertiii{T}\vertiii{VB} \leq orm{(AU)^*}_e orm{(VB)^*}_e \vertiii{T} ,\]

where the last inequality follows since \(\vertiii{S} \leq orm{S^*}_e\) for all \(S \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\). Since

\[ egin{aligned} orm{(AU)^*}_e orm{(VB)^*}_e &\leq orm{(AU)^*} orm{(VB)^*} \leq orm{A} orm{U} orm{V} orm{B} \leq (1 + \varepsilon),\end{aligned}\]

we get

\[1 \leq orm{(AU)^*}_e orm{(VB)^*}_e \vertiii{T} \leq (1 + \varepsilon) \vertiii{T}.\]

As this is true for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), it follows that \(1 \leq \vertiii{T}\), which proves the result.

□
9.

Automatic continuity of homomorphism from \(\mathscr{B}(C([0,\alpha]))\)

−

We show how a simple argument allows us to extend Ogden's result on automatic continuity to all ordinals. We first establish some auxiliary results.

For a Banach algebra \(\mathcal{B}\), we denote by \(\mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B})\) the Banach algebra of \((n imes n)\)-matrices whose entries are elements of \(\mathcal{B}\). We write \(T = [T_{i,j}]_{i,j=1}^n \in \mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B})\) for the matrix having \(T_{i,j} \in \mathcal{B}\) for its \((i,j)\)-entry. Denote by \(\pi_{i,j}: \mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B}) o \mathcal{B}\), \([T_{r,s}]_{r,s=1}^n \mapsto T_{i,j}\) (the map sending a matrix to its \((i,j)\)-entry) and \(\iota_{i,j}: \mathcal{B} o \mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B})\) the map sending an element \(T \in \mathcal{B}\) to the matrix with all entries zero except \(T\) in the \((i,j)\)-entry. We assume \(\mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B})\) is equipped with any norm \( orm{\cdot}\) satisfying

\[\max \{ orm{T_{i,j}}: 1 \leq i,j \leq n\} \leq orm{T} \leq \sum_{i,j = 1}^n orm{T_{i,j}},\]

so that both \(\iota_{i,j}\) and \(\pi_{i,j}\) are continuous.

Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a unital Banach algebra. Then every homomorphism from \(\mathcal{B}\) to a Banach algebra is continuous if and only if every homomorphism from \(\mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B})\) to a Banach algebra is continuous for every \(n \geq 1\).

ProofFold proof

The reverse direction is immediate, so we only need to show that if every homomorphism from \(\mathcal{B}\) to a Banach algebra is continuous, the same holds for \(\mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B})\), \(n \geq 2\).

Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a Banach algebra and \( heta: \mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B}) o \mathcal{A}\) be a homomorphism. Since \(\sum_{i,j=1}^n \iota_{i,j} \circ \pi_{i,j} = \identity_{\mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B})}\), it follows that

\[ heta = \sum_{i,j = 1}^n ( heta \circ \iota_{i,j}) \circ \pi_{i,j},\]

and since \(\pi_{i,j}\) is continuous, to prove continuity of \( heta\), it is enough to show continuity of \( heta_{i,j} = heta \circ \iota_{i,j}: \mathcal{B} o \mathcal{A}\) for each pair \(1 \leq i,j \leq n\).

Note that \( heta_{i,j}\) is linear. Furthermore, for \(1 \leq i \leq n\), \(\iota_{i,i}\) is an algebra homomorphism; therefore \( heta_{i,i}\) is an algebra homomorphism and thus continuous by hypothesis.

We focus now on the off-diagonal terms. Let \(i ot = j\) be fixed. For any \(S, U \in \mathcal{B}\) we have

\[ egin{aligned} heta_{i,j}(SU) &= heta(\iota_{i,j}(SU)) = heta(\iota_{i,i}(S)\iota_{i,j}(U)) \ &= heta(\iota_{i,i}(S)) heta(\iota_{i,j}(U)) = heta_{i,i}(S) heta_{i,j}(U).\end{aligned}\]

For any null-sequence \((S_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}\), it follows that

\[ heta_{i,j}(S_k) = heta_{i,i}(S_k) heta_{i,j}(\identity_\mathcal{B}) o 0\]

as \(k o \infty\), where we used that \( heta_{i,i}\) is continuous. This proves the continuity of \( heta_{i,j}\) and finishes the proof.

□

We remark in passing that the assumption that the Banach algebra \(\mathcal{B}\) is unital can be substantially weakened. In particular, it is enough that null sequences in \(\mathcal{B}\) factor.

Expressing the operators on \(X^n = X \oplus X \oplus \dots \oplus X\) in matrix form, we have \(\mathscr{B}(X^n) = \mathbb{M}_n(\mathscr{B}(X))\) and thus we get the following.

Let \(X\) be a Banach space. Then the operator norm is maximal in \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) if and only if the operator norm is maximal in \(\mathscr{B}(X^n)\) for every \(n \geq 1\).

We also recall the classification theorem for spaces of continuous functions on ordinals, originally proven by ; the specific formulation we give is taken from .

(Classification theorem of ordinal spaces)

Let \(\alpha < eta\) be two ordinals of the same cardinality, and let \(\xi\) be the first ordinal of this cardinality. Write \(\alpha = \xi\eta_1 + ho_1\) and \( eta = \xi\eta_2 + ho_2\) (\( ho_1 < \xi, ho_2 < \xi\)). Then there are two cases:

  1. If the cardinality of \(\alpha\) is an uncountable regular cardinal and \(\eta_1 \leq \xi\), then \(C([0, \alpha])\) is isomorphic to \(C([0, eta])\) iff \(\eta_1\) and \(\eta_2\) have the same cardinality.

  2. Otherwise, \(C([0, \alpha])\) is isomorphic to \(C([0, eta])\) iff \( eta < \alpha^\omega\) (where \(\omega\) is the first infinite ordinal).

Proof of Theorem 1.3Fold proof

We start with the observation that \(C([0, \alpha2])\) is naturally isomorphic to \(C([0, \alpha])\oplus C([0, \alpha])\). It follows from Johnson's automatic continuity result that whenever \(C([0, \alpha2]) \sim C([0, \alpha])\), then all homomorphisms from \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \alpha]))\) into a Banach algebra are continuous. By the Classification Theorem 9.3, the only cases when this does not hold (up to isomorphism of the space of continuous functions) is when \(\alpha\) is finite or \(\alpha = \xi n\) where \(\xi\) is the first ordinal with the same cardinality as \(\alpha\), the cardinality of \(\alpha\) is an uncountable regular cardinal and \(n \in \mathbb{N}\). The finite case is obvious, while in the latter case \(C([0, \alpha]) \sim C([0, \xi])^n\) and Ogden's theorem gives that every homomorphism from \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \xi]))\) to a Banach algebra is continuous. The result now follows from Corollary 9.2.

results.statementHtml: Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and consider the Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K))/\mathscr{K}(C_0(K))\). Then the essential norm \(\norm{\cdot}_e\) is minimal. In particular, the Calkin algebra admits a unique complete algebra norm.
Is there a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space \(K\) such that \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) admits a discontinuous homomorphism into a Banach algebra?
Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal. Then any homomorphism from \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \alpha]))\) into a Banach algebra is continuous.

Let \(\alpha\) be an ordinal. Then the algebra of operators \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \alpha]))\) and the Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C([0, \alpha]))/\mathscr{K}(C([0, \alpha]))\) admit an unique algebra norm.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and consider the Calkin algebra \(\mathscr{B}(C_0(K))/\mathscr{K}(C_0(K))\). Then the dual essential norm \(T \mapsto \norm{T^*}_e\) has Bonsall's minimality property.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and let \(X\) be a Banach space that does not contain a copy of \(\ell^1\) or for which the unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact. Then for any non-compact operator \(T: C_0(K) o X\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exist operators \(U \in \mathscr{B}(X, c_0)\) and \(V \in \mathscr{B}(c_0, C_0(K))\) such that

\[UTV = I_{c_0} \hspace{5pt} ext{ and } \hspace{5pt} orm{U} orm{V} < rac{2}{ orm{T}_e} + \varepsilon.\]

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and let \(X\) be a Banach space that does not contain a copy of \(\ell^1\) or for which the unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact. Then for any non-compact operator \(T: C_0(K) o X\)

\[ orm{T^*}_e = \sup \{ orm{U}^{-1} orm{V}^{-1}: UTV = I_{c_0} \}.\]

Theorem 1.6 could also be derived from Theorem 1.7 together with a duality result due to S. Axler, N. Jewell, and A. Shields . Although their result is stated only for the case where the domain and codomain coincide, a careful reading of the proof shows that it suffices for the dual of the domain to have the \(\lambda\)-metric approximation property for their argument to go through.

If \(K\) has an accumulation point, i.e. if \(C_0(K) ot = c_0(\Gamma)\), the constant \(2\) is sharp in Theorem 1.6, since in this case there exists an operator \(T \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) such that \( orm{T}_e = 2\) while \( orm{T^*}_e = 1\). Clearly, if \(C_0(K) = c_0(\Gamma)\) we have \( orm{T}_e = orm{T^*}_e\).

results.statementHtml: Let \(K\) be a locally compact Hausdorff space and \(X\) be a Banach space. Then an operator \(T: C_0(K) \to X\) is non-weakly compact if and only if \(T\) fixes a copy of \(c_0\).

In light of Pełczyński's theorem, one might hope that the assumption that \(K\) is scattered in Theorem 1.6 could be removed by replacing non-compactness with non-weak compactness. However, this is not possible, as \(\varepsilon( \cdot )\) is not comparable in general with the weak essential norm \(\norm{\cdot}_w\). Details of this will appear elsewhere.

results.statementHtml:
Let \(T \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K), X)\) where \(K\) is a locally compact Hausdorff space and \(X\) is a Banach space for which the unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact, and let \(\delta > 0\).

Then \(C_0(K)\) contains a sequence \((\eta_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}\) such that

\[\sup_{k \in K} \sum_{n=1}^\infty |\eta_n(k)| \leq 1 \hspace{5pt} ext{ and } \hspace{5pt} \inf_{n \in \mathbb{N}} orm{T\eta_n} > \delta\]

if and only if there are operators \(U \in \mathscr{B}(X, c_0)\) and \(V \in \mathscr{B}(c_0, C_0(K))\) such that

\[UTV = I_{c_0} \hspace{5pt} ext{ and } \hspace{5pt} orm{U} orm{V} < 1/\delta.\]

results.title: Hagler and Johnson
results.statementHtml: Let \(X\) be a Banach space. If \(X^*\) contains a closed subspace in which no normalized sequence converges weak\(^*\) to zero, then \(\ell^1\) is isomorphic to a subspace of \(X\).

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space, \(X\) be a Banach space, \(T: C_0(K) \to X\) be an operator with \(\norm{T}_e = 1\) and \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\). Then there exists a sequence of disjoint functions \((\eta_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset B_{C_0(K)}\) such that \(\norm{T\eta_j} > \delta\) for all \(j \in \mathbb{N}\).
A family of sets \(\mathcal{A}\) is called pairwise disjoint if \(A \cap B = \emptyset\) for any distinct \(A, B \in \mathcal{A}\).

Given a subset \(F \subset K\), we say that \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{T}\) is a neighbourhood collection around \(F\) if there exists a bijection \(U: F \to \mathcal{U}\) such that \(k \in U(k)\) for each \(k \in F\).

We define the support of \(\mathcal{U} \subset \mathcal{T}\) as

\[S(\mathcal{U}) = \bigcup_{U \in \mathcal{U}} U,\]

in other words, the set of those points \(k \in K\) which belong to some member of \(\mathcal{U}\).

Let \(A\) be any set, we denote \(\finset{A} = \{B \subset A: |B| < \omega\}\) and \(\inset{A} = \{B \subset A: |B| \leq \omega \}\), in other words, the collections of finite and countable subsets of \(A\), respectively.
Let \(F \in \finset{K}\), then there exists a pairwise disjoint neighbourhood collection around \(F\).

Let \(F \in \finset{K}\) and let \(\mathcal{U} \in \finset{\mathcal{T}}\) be a pairwise disjoint neighbourhood collection around \(F\). We define

\[\proj(\mathcal{U}, F) = \sum_{k \in F} \delta_{k} \otimes \id{U(k)},\]

where \(\delta_k: C_0(K) \to \mathbb{K}\) is the evaluation functional at \(k\), \(\id{U}\) denotes the indicator function of \(U\) and \(\delta_{k} \otimes \id{U(k)}\) denotes the rank-one operator defined via \(f \mapsto f(k)\id{U(k)}\).

1. \(\proj(\mathcal{U}, F)\) is a finite-rank projection.

  2. \(\norm{\proj(\mathcal{U}, F)} = 1\), except in the trivial case where \(F = \emptyset\). Hence \(\norm{I - \proj(\mathcal{U}, F)} \leq 2\).

  3. For any \(k \in F\), the adjoint projection satisfies \(\proj(\mathcal{U}, F)^* \delta_{k} = \delta_{k}\).
Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space. Then \(C_0(K)^* \cong \ell^1(K)\).

Let \(\mu \in C_0(K)^*\), we call the subset

\[\supp({\mu}) = \{k \in K: \mu(\{k\}) \not = 0\}\]

the support of \(\mu\).

For \(C \subset K\), we define the restriction operator \(R_C: C_0(K)^* \to C_0(K)^*\), acting on \(\mu \in C_0(K)^*\) by

\[R_C \mu = \sum_{k \in C} \mu(\{ k \})\delta_k.\]

Let \(\{C_1, C_2, \dots, C_N\}\) be pairwise disjoint subsets of \(K\) and set \(C = igsqcup_{n=1}^N C_n\). Then:

  1. \(R_{C} = \sum_{n=1}^N R_{C_n}\), in particular, \( orm{\sum_{n=1}^N R_{C_n}} = orm{R_C} = 1\).

  2. For any \(\mu \in C_0(K)^*\), we have \( orm{\sum_{n=1}^N R_{C_n} \mu} = \sum_{n=1}^N orm{R_{C_n} \mu}\).

Let \(\eta \in C_0(K)\), we define the zero set of \(\eta\) by

\[\mathbf{Z}(\eta) = \{k \in K: \eta(k) = 0 \} = \eta^{-1}(\{0\}),\]

and similarly

\[\nonvan{\eta} = K \backslash \mathbf{Z}(\eta) = \{k \in K: \eta(k) \not = 0 \}.\]

Further, we say that \(\eta\) vanishes at a set \(F \subset K\) if \(F \subset \mathbf{Z}(\eta)\).

There exist \((x^*_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset B_{X^*}\) and finite sets \(F_j \subset \Tsupp{x^*_j}\) satisfying the following properties:

  1. \(F_i \cap F_j = \emptyset\) when \(i \not = j\), or in other words, the family \((F_j)_{j=1}^\infty\) is pairwise disjoint.

  2. \(\norm{R_{F_j} T^* x_j^*} > \delta + 2\theta\) for all \(j \in \mathbb{N}\).

For later reference, we observe that the condition \(\delta < 1/2\) stems from the fact that, to define \(\eta_{J+1}\), we need to consider \((I - \proj(\mathcal{U}_J, A_J))\zeta_{J+1}\) whose norm may be greater than one, but it is at most two by Lemma 4.7 (b).

Let \((x^*_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset B_{X^*}\) and let \((F_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset \finset{K}\) be pairwise disjoint. Then, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exist \(n \in \mathbb{N}\) and a pairwise disjoint neighbourhood collection \(\mathcal{U}_n\) around \(F_n\) with the property that for all \(J \in \mathbb{N}\), there exists \(j > J\) with \(\norm{R_{S(\mathcal{U}_n)} T^* x^*_j} < \varepsilon\).

Let \((x^*_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset B_{X^*}\) and let \((F_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset \finset{K}\) be pairwise disjoint. Then for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exist \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), a pairwise disjoint neighbourhood collection \(\mathcal{U}_n\) around \(F_n\) and a subsequence \((x^*_{k_j})_{j=1}^\infty\) of \((x^*_{j})_{j=1}^\infty\) such that \(\lVert R_{S(\mathcal{U}_n)} T^* x^*_{k_j} \rVert < \varepsilon\) for all \(j \in \mathbb{N}\).

There exist \((y^*_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset B_{X^*}\), finite sets \(A_j \subset \Tsupp{y^*_j}\), and pairwise disjoint neighbourhood collections \(\mathcal{V}_j\) around \(A_j\) satisfying:

  1. The family \(\bigcup_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{V}_j\) is pairwise disjoint; that is \(U \cap V = \emptyset\) for any distinct \(U, V \in \bigcup_{j=1}^\infty \mathcal{V}_j\).

  2. \(\norm{R_{A_j} T^* y_j^*} > \delta + \theta\) for each \(j \in \mathbb{N}\).

Let \(\delta \in (0, \norm{T^*}_e)\) and fix \(\theta\) such that \(\delta + 2\theta < \norm{T^*}_e\). Then there exist \((x^*_j)_{j=1}^\infty \subset B_{X^*}\) and finite sets \(F_j \subset \Tsupp{x^*_j}\) satisfying conditions (a) and (b) of Proposition 5.2.

The essence of the argument is the following: while in \(C_0(K)\) the possible presence of accumulation points only allows for the bound \(\norm{I - \proj(\mathcal{U}, F)} \leq 2\), in the dual case \(C_0(K)^* \cong \ell^1(K)\) we have a natural way to project. Namely, in the dual formulation, the role of \(\proj(\mathcal{U}, F)\) is played by \(R_{F}\) and thus we can guarantee \(\norm{I - R_F} = 1\) by Lemma 4.11.

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space and let \(X\) be a Banach space that does not contain a copy of \(\ell^1\) or for which the unit ball of \(X^*\) is weak\(^*\) sequentially compact. Then for any non-compact operator \(T: C_0(K) o X\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exist operators \(U \in \mathscr{B}(X, c_0)\) and \(V \in \mathscr{B}(c_0, C_0(K))\) such that

\[UTV = I_{c_0} \hspace{5pt} ext{ and } \hspace{5pt} orm{U} orm{V} < rac{1}{ orm{T^*}_e} + \varepsilon.\]

Let \(K\) be a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space. Then, there exist \(A \in \mathscr{B}(c_0, C_0(K))\) and \(B \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K), c_0)\) such that

\[BA = I_{c_0} \hspace{10pt} \text{ and } \norm{A} = \norm{B} = 1.\]

There exists a sequence of non-compact operators \((P_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) such that, for every sequence of operators \((T_n)_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) with \(\norm{T_n}_e > 2^{2n+1}\) for every \(n \in \mathbb{N}\), there exist \(U, V \in \mathscr{B}(C_0(K))\) such that

\[P_n U T_n V P_n = P_n \hspace{10 pt} \text{ for all } n \in \mathbb{N}.\]

The previous argument works in a more general setting. Namely, let \(X\), \(Y\) be Banach spaces. For \(T \in \mathscr{B}(X)\) define

\[ u_Y{(T)} = \sup\{ orm{U}^{-1} orm{V}^{-1}: UTV = I_Y\}\]

if \(I_Y\) factors through \(T\) and \( u_Y{(T)} = 0\) otherwise. Further, let \(\mathcal{J}_Y = \{T \in \mathscr{B}(X): u_Y(T) = 0\}\), in other words, the set of operators that do not factor \(I_Y\). Observe that the set \(\mathcal{J}_Y\) is always closed.

Suppose that \(\mathcal{J}_Y\) is closed under addition (and thus, a closed ideal of \(\mathscr{B}(X)\)) and that \(Y\) admits a Schauder decomposition \((Y_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) with \(\sup \{d_{BM}(Y_n, Y) : n \geq 1\} < \infty\), where \(d_{BM}\) denotes the Banach-Mazur distance. Then \( u_Y\) minorizes any algebra norm on \(\mathscr{B}(X)/\mathcal{J}_Y\). In particular, if \( u_Y\) defines an algebra norm, it is minimal.

Further, note that the conditions on \(Y\) are satisfied, for example, by the classical sequence spaces \(\ell^p\), \(1 \leq p \leq \infty\).

These factorisation-type norms arise naturally in algebras of the form \(\mathscr{B}(X)/\mathscr{I}\) for some ideal \(\mathscr{I}\) and play a central role in the study of their norm properties. For example, in a forthcoming paper, Johnson and Phillips introduce the notion of uniform incompressibility (see also for a definition), and employ factorization-type norms to show this property holds in multiple Banach algebra of the form \(\mathscr{B}(X)/\mathscr{I}\). Our results show that the essential norm is uniformly incompressible for the Calkin algebra of \(C_0(K)\) spaces, \(K\) a scattered, locally compact Hausdorff space.

Let \(\mathcal{B}\) be a unital Banach algebra. Then every homomorphism from \(\mathcal{B}\) to a Banach algebra is continuous if and only if every homomorphism from \(\mathbb{M}_n(\mathcal{B})\) to a Banach algebra is continuous for every \(n \geq 1\).
Let \(X\) be a Banach space. Then the operator norm is maximal in \(\mathscr{B}(X)\) if and only if the operator norm is maximal in \(\mathscr{B}(X^n)\) for every \(n \geq 1\).

results.title: Classification theorem of ordinal spaces
results.statementHtml:
Let \(\alpha < \beta\) be two ordinals of the same cardinality, and let \(\xi\) be the first ordinal of this cardinality. Write \(\alpha = \xi\eta_1 + \rho_1\) and \(\beta = \xi\eta_2 + \rho_2\) (\(\rho_1 < \xi,\rho_2 < \xi\)). Then there are two cases:

  1. If the cardinality of \(\alpha\) is an uncountable regular cardinal and \(\eta_1 \leq \xi\), then \(C([0, \alpha])\) is isomorphic to \(C([0, \beta])\) iff \(\eta_1\) and \(\eta_2\) have the same cardinality.

  2. Otherwise, \(C([0, \alpha])\) is isomorphic to \(C([0, \beta])\) iff \(\beta < \alpha^\omega\) (where \(\omega\) is the first infinite ordinal).

theorem-1-1.note: Both conclusions are proved: minimality of the essential norm and uniqueness of the complete algebra norm. The statement includes finite as well as infinite K.

theorem-1-3.note: Proved for arbitrary ordinals over the real or complex field. Continuity is a conclusion; neither the homomorphism nor the Banach algebra is assumed unital.

corollary-1-4.note: Both the operator algebra and the Calkin algebra are covered. The competing algebra norm need not be complete. Uniqueness means equivalence of norms.

theorem-1-5.note: Bonsall minimality is proved for the dual essential norm: every algebra norm dominated by it agrees with it.

theorem-1-6.note: The strict bound and both alternatives for X are proved. No additional factorisation or representation hypothesis remains.

theorem-1-7.note: The exact supremum formula is proved for both alternatives for X. IsLUB expresses the least-upper-bound property, without assuming the supremum is attained.

theorem-3-1.label: factorizationFromDisjointFunctions
theorem-3-1.note: The proved consequence used here starts with disjoint unit-ball functions and a strict uniform lower bound. It gives the required factorisation for either alternative for X. The full equivalence for an arbitrary sequence satisfying the pointwise sum bound is not a theorem in this project.

theorem-3-3.note: The normalized disjoint-function theorem is proved from the scattered, locally compact Hausdorff hypotheses. DisjointFunctionsHalf spells out the norm-one normalization and the interval 0 < δ < 1/2.

lemma-4-5.note: For any finite family of distinct points, the proof constructs pairwise disjoint compact clopen neighbourhoods. This is the stronger form used throughout Sections 4–6.

definition-4-2.note: This finite, indexed structure includes compact clopen neighbourhoods and pairwise disjointness, combining Definitions 4.1–4.2 with the convention in Section 4.

definition-4-6.note: The finite-rank operator is the sum of the point evaluations multiplied by the corresponding compact clopen indicators. Its projection and norm properties are proved in Lemma 4.7.

lemma-4-7.note: All three clauses are proved. The norm-one assertion has the necessary nonempty-family hypothesis; the estimate for I − P holds for every finite family.

proofs.label: (b) Norm one for a nonempty family

theorem-4-8.note: The isometric dual representation is proved over either scalar field, with point masses identified with evaluation functionals. The proof treats locally compact K directly.

definition-4-10.note: Restriction is defined in the atomic representation of the dual: retain the coordinates in C and set the others to zero. Rudin.lean proves that this representation exists.

lemma-4-11.note: The restriction identity and norm additivity are proved for two disjoint sets, giving the finite version by iteration. The general operator estimate recorded here is ≤ 1. Equality requires a nonempty union; it does not hold for the empty restriction.

proposition-5-2.note: The finite-atom construction is proved in atomic coordinates. Its representation hypothesis is established by exists_atomicDualModel; the displayed threshold is the Section 5 bound.

lemma-5-4.note: The essential-weight argument is proved for a bounded operator into ℓ¹(K). Substituting the atomic form of T* gives the paper’s statement.

corollary-5-5.note: Both the subsequence selection in atomic coordinates and its application to T* are proved.

lemma-6-1.note: The infinite diagonal selection is proved in atomic coordinates, from pairwise disjoint finite pieces of sufficiently large mass. The chosen neighbourhoods are disjoint across all stages.

proposition-7-1.note: The dual finite-piece construction is proved for every threshold below ‖T*‖ₑ. The atomic representation appearing in the statement is proved in Rudin.lean.

lemma-8-1.note: The norm-one complemented copy of c₀ is proved for infinite K. That hypothesis is necessary: finite K gives a finite-dimensional C₀(K). The main theorems handle finite K separately.

lemma-8-2.note: The simultaneous factorisation is proved for an orthogonal c₀ block family and the individual factorisation theorem. The completed main proof constructs that family from the complemented c₀ copy and proves the individual factorisations. Choosing ρₙ = 2⁻ⁿ gives the paper’s thresholds.

theorem-3-2.label: dualNormalizedBlockNull_of_not_containsEllOne
theorem-3-2.note: The formal argument proves the normalized weak* null block consequence needed when X contains no copy of ℓ¹. This is the part used in the factorisation proof; the cited closed-subspace formulation is not separately stated.

proposition-9-1.label: continuous_matrix_hom_of_corners
proposition-9-1.note: The substantive forward implication is proved by the diagonal-corner argument for every finite matrix algebra. The reverse implication in the paper follows by taking n = 1; it is not packaged as a separate equivalence.

corollary-9-2.label: continuous_operator_hom_of_finitePower
corollary-9-2.note: The finite-power transfer used in Section 9 is proved at the level of automatic continuity. This declaration is not the paper’s norm-maximality equivalence itself.

theorem-9-3.label: ordinalSpaceReduction
theorem-9-3.note: The project proves the classification consequence needed for Theorem 1.3: the space is finite-dimensional, isomorphic to its square, or isomorphic to a positive finite power of the space on a regular uncountable initial ordinal. The full two-way classification printed here is not formalised.

question-1-2.note: This is a question posed by the paper. The project does not claim an answer.

theorem-1-10.note: The Lean formalisation bypasses Pełczyński’s general theorem. Under the hypotheses of Theorems 1.6 and 1.7, the required factorisations are constructed directly from disjoint functions. The full equivalence stated in the paper is neither proved nor assumed as an axiom in this project.

remark-1-8.note: This describes an alternative route through a cited duality theorem. The completed proof of Theorem 1.6 uses the direct disjoint-function construction instead.

remark-1-9.note: The sharpness examples in this remark are not separately formalised. The factor-two upper bound itself is proved in Theorem 1.6.

remark-1-11.note: This discusses a proposed extension and work elsewhere. No formal theorem for this discussion is recorded in this project.

definition-4-1.note: Pairwise disjointness is expressed by Pairwise (fun i j => Disjoint (U i) (U j)). For sets, Disjoint means that their intersection is empty. The fields of NeighborhoodFamily use this condition.

definition-4-3.note: The support of an indexed neighbourhood family U is written ⋃ i, U.sets i. This union is used directly in the essential-weight and diagonal-selection statements; there is no separate named definition.

definition-4-4.note: Finite subsets are represented by Finset K. Countability of a subset A is expressed by A.Countable. These are existing notions in Lean’s libraries, rather than new definitions of this paper.

definition-4-9.note: In atomic coordinates, the support of μ is Function.support (M.representation μ). The representation theorem identifies these coefficients with point masses; atomicDual_countable_support proves the support is countable.

definition-5-1.note: Function.support η denotes {k | η k ≠ 0}; its complement is the zero set. Vanishing on F is written as a pointwise condition ∀ k ∈ F, η k = 0. The constructions use these expressions directly.

remark-5-3.note: The bound ‖I − P‖ ≤ 2 is proved in norm_id_sub_neighborhoodProjection_le_two, linked under Lemma 4.7. It accounts for the threshold δ < 1/2.

remark-7-2.note: The coordinate restriction onto a complement has norm at most one, as proved in norm_id_sub_restrictionL1_le. This is the estimate used by the dual argument. Equality needs a nonempty complement.

remark-8-3.note: Parts of the argument are developed for general factor spaces, but the entire Schauder-decomposition generalisation and all its examples are not recorded as a theorem in this project.

remark-8-4.note: This places the result among related work on uniform incompressibility. The main minimality theorems are formalised; the bibliographical discussion is not a separate Lean theorem.

corollary-7-3.label: theorem_1_7
corollary-7-3.note: The sharp supremum theorem gives this epsilon estimate by choosing a factorisation value sufficiently close to ‖T*‖ₑ. The project’s general result is stated as Theorem 1.7; the separately named epsilon lemma treats the C₀(K) endomorphism case.

footnote.html: In Alspach and Benyamini, Primariness of spaces of continuous functions on ordinals (1977), p. 65, the inequality \(\eta<\xi\) (\(\eta_1<\xi\) here) is misprinted as \(\eta\leq\xi\).
